analysis.one_liner: Lets people sickened by glyphosate or elemental phosphorus sue the manufacturers and strips a federal order shielding them.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan cosponsors but referred to the House Judiciary Committee and given no hearing or vote so far.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two things. First, it would bar any federal money from carrying out a February 2026 executive order that put federal weight behind producing elemental phosphorus and glyphosate weed killer under wartime-style defense production powers. Second, it would create a new right to sue: anyone who got sick or died from exposure to these chemicals could take the manufacturers, distributors, and sellers to federal court for compensatory and punitive damages, and the bill would knock out any defense the companies might claim from working under that executive order or as government contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: People who were exposed to glyphosate herbicides or elemental phosphorus and became ill, along with their families and estates, would gain a clear federal right to sue the companies that made, distributed, or sold the chemicals, including for punitive damages and legal fees. It also preserves state-law claims and keeps pending lawsuits alive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to glyphosate and their families

how_it_helps.text: Creates an explicit federal cause of action letting anyone injured, sickened, or killed by exposure to elemental phosphorus or a glyphosate herbicide sue any entity that manufactured, distributed, formulated, supplied, or sold the chemical, with federal courts required to hear the case regardless of amount in controversy.
Allows courts to award compensatory damages including medical expenses and lost income, punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees.

Waives and nullifies any immunity the companies might claim under section 707 of the Defense Production Act or any other law, and expressly bars a 'federal contractor defense' based on compliance with the February 2026 executive order.
Prohibits the use of any federal funds to implement, administer, or enforce the executive order on phosphorus and glyphosate supply issued February 18, 2026.
Preserves all existing and pending lawsuits and does not preempt stronger state-law remedies.

analysis.who_pays: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, along with distributors, formulators, and sellers, would bear litigation and damages liability. Farmers and other glyphosate users could face higher prices or supply disruption if federal defense-production support ends or liability costs are passed through.
analysis.who_pays_short: Glyphosate makers, sellers, and their customers

drawbacks.text: The causation standard is low: a plaintiff only has to show the injury was caused 'in whole or in part' by exposure, which could support a very large volume of lawsuits against makers, distributors, co-ops, and retailers, and raise costs that get passed to farmers and consumers.

The scientific question of whether ordinary glyphosate exposure causes disease is contested; a federal cause of action written this broadly would leave those disputes to juries, with potentially unpredictable results for a chemical widely used in agriculture.
Ending federal funds for the executive order could disrupt the federal effort to secure domestic supply of elemental phosphorus and glyphosate that the order was meant to address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who believe their illness came from these chemicals, the bill is a strong remedy: it guarantees a courtroom, real damages, and lawyers' fees, and it removes immunity shields the executive order could have created. The honest cost is litigation risk and potential price or supply effects for a chemical American agriculture uses at scale, and the broad 'in whole or in part' causation language makes the scope of liability hard to predict. The bill is deliberately sweeping; whether that sweep is a feature or a flaw depends largely on how one weighs the scientific evidence on glyphosate harm.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Massie introduced the bill in the House on February 20, 2026.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is where the action history ends.
Sixteen members cosponsored it: twelve of the 217 House Democrats and four of the 223 House Republicans.
No committee action, vote, or further step appears in the record as of the latest action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Glyphosate and phosphorus manufacturers, so far: the bill has gone nowhere, and the February 2026 executive order it targets remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Glyphosate and phosphorus makers, so far

for.name: Reps. Chellie Pingree, Ro Khanna, Nancy Mace, and Lauren Boebert
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 20, 2026 and has taken no further action: no hearing or markup scheduled in the record.

against.name: The President
against.what_they_did: Issued the February 18, 2026 executive order directing federal support for elemental phosphorus and glyphosate production, which the bill seeks to defund and neutralize in court.

against.name: Glyphosate manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Have long sought federal protection from cancer and injury lawsuits over glyphosate products, which this bill would foreclose.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican often at odds with his own party, and the 16 cosponsors split 12 of 217 Democrats and 4 of 223 Republicans, so support crosses party lines but is thin on both sides.

industries.note: The bill gives exposed people a federal right to sue them for compensatory and punitive damages and strips any immunity they could claim from the executive order or government-contractor status. Their interest in keeping the executive order's protections runs directly against the public's ability to seek compensation for injury.

They face the same new federal cause of action and lose the federal funding behind the defense-production executive order. Their interest in federal immunity runs against injured plaintiffs' interests.

'Covered entity' is defined to include distributors, formulators, suppliers, and sellers, not just manufacturers, so co-ops, farm suppliers, and retailers could be sued as well. Their interest in being shielded runs against the public's right to sue.

The bill does not ban glyphosate, but ending federal defense-production support and adding liability costs could affect price or availability of a herbicide many farms depend on. Their interest does not clearly run with or against the public here.

analysis.trajectory: A House-only bill with 16 cosponsors that has sat in the Judiciary Committee since the day it was introduced faces long odds: most bills referred to committee never get a hearing or a floor vote, and there is no sign of leadership support here. Barring a push that the record does not show, it is likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress.
